title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year
oneLiner: Whether the federal government should cap net arrivals below the levels of the past decade and well below the post-pandemic peak.
body: Net overseas migration is arrivals minus departures of people who stay, or leave, for at least twelve months. It averaged just over 200,000 a year in the decade before the pandemic and exceeded 500,000 in 2022–23. The proposal is a cap of 200,000, which would require the government to manage the student, temporary-work and permanent programs together to hit it.
contextBackground:
Australia sets an annual permanent migration program but does not directly cap [net overseas migration](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/population/overseas-migration/latest-release), most of which is temporary: students, working-holiday makers and temporary skilled workers. The post-pandemic rebound pushed net migration above 500,000 in 2022–23. At the 2025 election the Coalition pledged to cut it to 160,000; the [May 2026 budget](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/our-insights/gms-flash-alert/2026/flash-alert-2026-124.html) forecasts 295,000 for 2025–26, 245,000 for 2026–27 and 225,000 a year from 2027–28.

The lever both parties reach for is international students. A [2026 planning level of 295,000](https://theconversation.com/australias-student-caps-will-ease-up-in-2026-but-times-will-still-be-tough-for-international-education-262521) new students applies through visa-processing 'slow lanes' because the Senate rejected legislated caps in 2024; the Coalition proposes 240,000; and from [2 October 2026](https://www.ed.events/post/international-students-australias-intensifying-migration-debate) most student visa applicants may no longer bring partners or children.
contextDisagreement: Both sides accept that 2022–23 was exceptional and that housing is the pressure point, and the forecast is already falling towards 225,000. The real dispute is whether the last 25,000 to 65,000 a year should come out of international education, which is the only component large enough to cut, and what that costs.

timeline.label: 2010s
timeline.text: Net overseas migration runs at roughly 200,000 to 250,000 a year, driven mainly by students and temporary workers.
Borders close. Net migration turns negative for the first time since the Second World War.
Reopened borders produce a record intake above 500,000 as students and temporary workers return.

timeline.label: Nov 2024
timeline.text: The Senate rejects legislated international student caps; the government moves to 'planning levels' enforced through visa processing.

timeline.label: May 2025
timeline.text: The Coalition takes a pledge to cut net migration to 160,000 to the election and loses.

timeline.label: Aug 2025
timeline.text: The 2026 planning level for new international students is set at 295,000, up from 270,000.

timeline.label: May 2026
timeline.text: The budget forecasts net overseas migration of 245,000 in 2026–27 and 225,000 a year from 2027–28.

timeline.label: 2 Oct 2026
timeline.text: Student visa changes limit onshore applications and bar most applicants from bringing partners or children.

otherClaim.title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade

claimItself.title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade
claimItself.oneLiner: Dwellings built per new resident have fallen, and vacancy rates in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth sit near record lows.
claimItself.body: Completions peaked around 2017 and fell through the pandemic as costs rose and builders failed, while population growth resumed at pace. The national housing agency's projections show a cumulative shortfall against household formation through the second half of the decade.

otherClaim.title: Grattan Institute estimates each unexpected extra 100,000 migrants lifts rents by about 1 per cent, and that cutting net migration to 160,000 would leave rents about 6 per cent lower after a decade

claimItself.title: Grattan Institute estimates each unexpected extra 100,000 migrants lifts rents by about 1 per cent, and that cutting net migration to 160,000 would leave rents about 6 per cent lower after a decade
claimItself.oneLiner: The best-known estimate of how much migration moves rents: real, and modest.
claimItself.body: Grattan's analysis of the Coalition's 2025 pledge found that holding net overseas migration at 160,000 a year would leave rents about 6 per cent lower than otherwise after ten years, and that cutting permanent skilled visas alone would leave them about 2.5 per cent lower, at a significant cost to incomes. It also noted the federal government has little direct control over net migration, which is driven by uncapped temporary visas.

otherClaim.title: The 2022–23 surge largely reflected students and temporary workers returning after two years of closed borders

claimItself.title: The 2022–23 surge largely reflected students and temporary workers returning after two years of closed borders
claimItself.oneLiner: Two cohorts arrived in one year because none arrived in the two before.
claimItself.body: Net migration was negative in 2020–21. When borders reopened, the students and temporary workers who would have come across two or three years arrived together, and departures were low because few had been in the country long enough to leave. The Centre for Population's projections show net migration falling back towards its long-run level without any change in policy.

otherClaim.title: Holding net overseas migration below 200,000 would require large cuts to international student numbers

claimItself.title: Holding net overseas migration below 200,000 would require large cuts to international student numbers
claimItself.oneLiner: Students are the biggest component of net migration, so a cap of this size is mostly a cap on them.
claimItself.body: Permanent skilled and family visas are already capped and make up a minority of net migration. The remainder is dominated by students, with working-holiday makers and temporary skilled workers behind them. Holding the total below 200,000 while keeping the permanent program at current levels leaves international education as the only component large enough to cut.

claimItself.oneLiner: The government's own shortage list shows the same occupations year after year.
claimItself.body: Jobs and Skills Australia's annual occupation shortage list has consistently included nurses, aged-care workers, electricians, carpenters and other trades. Employers in those sectors argue that skilled and temporary migration is the only way to staff them at current wages and training rates.

claimItself.title: The May 2026 budget forecasts net overseas migration falling to 245,000 in 2026–27 and 225,000 a year from 2027–28
claimItself.oneLiner: The number is already heading back to its pre-pandemic range without a cap.
claimItself.body: Budget forecasts put net overseas migration at 295,000 in 2025–26, 245,000 in 2026–27 and 225,000 a year thereafter, roughly the level of the decade before the pandemic. Treasury's long-run assumption is about 235,000. A cap of 200,000 would therefore bind by 25,000 to 45,000 a year on current forecasts.
